headline.headline: NATIONALS SURVIVE ASTROS IN 12-11 SLUGFEST AT NATIONALS PARK
headline.deck: Six home runs fly as Washington holds on after Houston nearly erases a six-run deficit
headline.body:
WASHINGTON — Nationals Park turned into a launching pad Monday night, and when the dust settled after nine wild innings, the Washington Nationals had outlasted the Houston Astros 12-11 in one of the summer's most chaotic afternoons of baseball. Six home runs left the yard, the lead changed hands repeatedly, and a six-run Washington fifth inning that seemed to put the game away was nearly swallowed whole by a four-run Houston eighth.

The Nationals built their foundation with a thunderous third inning, plating five runs to take a 6-4 lead after Houston had grabbed a 4-1 edge through the first two frames. CJ Abrams clubbed his 19th home run of the season, and Nathaniel Wood connected for his 24th blast to pace Washington's attack. For the Astros, Jose Altuve hit his ninth of the year and Yainer Diaz went deep for his fifth, but the Houston bats could not deliver the knockout blow when it mattered most.

The Astros pulled to within one run after a stunning four-run eighth inning that silenced the crowd of 11,092, with Derek Matthews adding his seventh home run and Curtis Mead his 15th to fuel the rally. But Washington's bullpen slammed the door in the ninth, preserving the victory and handing Houston a gut-punch loss in a game that featured doubles by Jordan Walker and Braden Shewmake among a combined 23 runs on the evening.

secondary.headline: METS STUN BRAVES IN TEN, 7-6, ON LATE RALLY
secondary.deck: New York scores three in the ninth and two more in the tenth to escape Atlanta
secondary.body:
ATLANTA — The New York Mets were three outs from defeat Monday night at Truist Park. Then they were one out from defeat in extra innings. Then they won. New York staged a three-run ninth-inning rally to tie the Atlanta Braves at 6-6, then pushed across two more runs in the tenth to escape with a 7-6 victory before a crowd of 31,445 that went from jubilant to stunned in the final three frames.

The game went ten innings and consumed three hours and 42 minutes. Fernando Peralta earned the win in relief while R. Lopez also factored into the decision. The Braves led 3-1 after three innings and 6-3 entering the ninth, only to watch the Mets claw back. Hit-by-pitch incidents involving J. Young and D. Baldwin added to the tension in a game that featured every element of a midsummer classic between two NL East rivals.

secondary.headline: FLAMES LOCK UP NEMEC ON FIVE-YEAR DEAL AS FREE AGENCY RESHAPES ROSTERS
secondary.deck: Calgary commits $36.25 million to young defenseman Simon Nemec in marquee signing
secondary.body:
CALGARY — The Calgary Flames wasted no time making their mark on NHL free agency, signing defenseman Simon Nemec to a five-year contract worth $36.25 million on Monday. The deal averages $7.25 million per season and signals Calgary's intent to build around young blue-line talent as the franchise looks to return to postseason relevance after sitting out the second round of this spring's playoffs.

Nemec, who brings puck-moving ability and two-way defensive instincts to the Flames back end, figures to anchor a Calgary defensive unit that needed an injection of youth and skill. The signing comes amid a broader NHL free agency frenzy that has already reshuffled rosters across the league, with teams spending aggressively to position themselves ahead of next season. Meanwhile, Washington's Alex Ovechkin said Monday he is uncertain when he will retire, with his wife suggesting he has one year remaining, maybe two.

secondary.headline: BREWERS ERUPT FOR FOUR IN SEVENTH, STEAL 4-3 WIN IN ST. LOUIS
secondary.deck: Milwaukee rallies from three-run deficit with a decisive seventh-inning burst
secondary.body:
ST. LOUIS — The Milwaukee Brewers trailed the St. Louis Cardinals 3-0 heading into the seventh inning Monday and had managed nothing against Cardinals pitching through six frames. Then, in a burst that lasted long enough to flip the scoreboard completely, the Brewers pushed across four runs in the seventh to steal a 4-3 victory at Busch Stadium before 21,786 fans.

The Cardinals had scored twice in the third and added a run in the sixth to build their cushion, but Milwaukee's bullpen shut St. Louis out over the final three innings after the offense did its work. A pinch runner was inserted for D. Hamilton in the decisive seventh frame, and a pinch hitter struck out for Pagé in the ninth as both teams used their benches freely in a game that took two hours and 45 minutes to complete.

column.headline: NATIONALS PARK REMINDED US WHY JULY BASEBALL IS WORTH STAYING UP FOR
column.body:
Twenty-three runs. Six home runs. A four-run eighth-inning rally that nearly made the whole thing come undone. Monday night in Washington was exactly the kind of game that gets described the next morning as exhausting and then rewatched on replay three more times before noon. The Nationals and Astros played the sort of baseball that no simulation can reproduce, the kind where every run feels earned and every out feels contested, and where the final score of 12-11 looks almost orderly compared to what actually happened on the field.

And yet on the same night in Atlanta, the Mets were pulling off a three-run ninth and stealing a ten-inning game that the Braves had every reason to believe was already won. July baseball does not wait for October to get interesting. Anyone who needed a reminder got two of them Monday night, delivered in full by teams that were supposed to be filling out the middle of a long summer schedule. Consider the message received.

story.headline: ROYALS TORCH PHILLIES, 15-1, AS THOMAS, PEREZ, TOLBERT AND MAILE ALL GO DEEP
story.deck: Kansas City erupts for six in the first, never looks back against Philadelphia
story.body:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The Kansas City Royals wasted no time Monday, sending six runs across the plate in the first inning and never letting up in a 15-1 demolition of the Philadelphia Phillies at Kauffman Stadium that left a crowd of 13,496 watching the home team pile on through all nine innings. Four Royals homers — by Lorenzo Thomas, Salvador Perez, Tolbert and Maile — punctuated a relentless offensive performance that had Philadelphia's pitching staff shredded before the second inning began.

Perez, who went deep for his 11th homer of the season, was hit by a pitch from Trivino III earlier in the contest, then came around to score in a seventh-inning rally that stretched the lead to double digits. Thomas added his sixth long ball of the year and Tolbert and Maile each went deep for their first of the season. Turner and Bohm each contributed doubles for Philadelphia in a losing effort, but the Phillies never threatened after scoring their lone run in the opening frame, stranding a staggering 23 baserunners across the game.

Winner Trivino III and Cruz combined to hold Philadelphia scoreless over the final eight innings while Kansas City added runs in every frame through the eighth. The Royals, who finished with 25 runners left on base themselves, kept the Phillies' pitchers working deep into the afternoon in a game that ran three hours and nine minutes. The loss dropped Philadelphia deeper into a difficult stretch, while Kansas City's lineup demonstrated the kind of top-to-bottom production that can make a contender dangerous heading into the second half of the season.

story.headline: CELTICS SHIP JAYLEN BROWN AS NBA'S SUMMER OF UPHEAVAL ROLLS ON
story.deck: Brad Stevens deals a cornerstone while Jokic plays the waiting game in Denver.
story.body:
The Boston Celtics have traded Jaylen Brown, president of basketball operations Brad Stevens announced Monday, with Stevens citing a "challenging" path forward as the reason for dealing one of the franchise's most decorated players. Stevens framed the move as a bid to keep the Celtics competitive while gaining roster flexibility and what he called "optionality" heading into an uncertain free agency landscape. The transaction sent shockwaves through a league already churning with summer activity.

In Denver, Nikola Jokic quietly dropped his own bombshell, confirming he will not sign a contract extension with the Nuggets this summer despite repeatedly stating his desire to remain in Colorado long term. The three-time MVP said he intends to wait until next summer to finalize any deal, leaving the Nuggets in an awkward holding pattern as rival franchises monitor the situation with barely concealed interest.

Meanwhile, the Las Vegas Summer League provided its own theater. Sixth overall pick Mikel Brown Jr. dazzled onlookers with a jaw-dropping wraparound dime that immediately circulated across social media, while Cam Boozer and Darryn Peterson engaged in a spirited 3-point exchange that had scouts reaching for their notebooks. The rookie showcase underscored just how quickly the NBA's next generation is announcing itself amid the chaos of the veteran landscape above them.

story.headline: ROBERTSON FILES FOR ARBITRATION AS NHL FREE AGENCY FRENZY RESHAPES ROSTERS
story.deck: Stars winger seeks big payday while Flames, Ducks lock up young defensive cornerstones.
story.body:
Jason Robertson, the Dallas Stars' leading scorer and one of the most dangerous wingers in the Western Conference, filed for salary arbitration Monday, setting up a potentially contentious summer showdown between the 25-year-old and Stars management. Robertson, who previously spurned a potential trade to the Seattle Kraken rather than sign a long-term extension, is now forcing Dallas into a formal hearing process that could result in a significant raise or an ugly divorce between a franchise and its most potent offensive weapon.

While Robertson's situation simmered, the Calgary Flames and Anaheim Ducks moved aggressively to secure their defensive futures. Calgary inked former second-overall pick Simon Nemec to a five-year, $36.25 million contract, betting that the 21-year-old Slovak blueliner will anchor their back end for the better part of the decade. Hours later, Anaheim locked up Pavel Mintyukov on a five-year deal, rewarding the young defenseman whose 17 goals and 52 assists over 204 career games have made him one of the brightest young stars on a Ducks team rapidly ascending toward contention.

Meanwhile, the hockey world continued to parse every word out of Washington regarding Alex Ovechkin, the all-time goals leader who will not commit to retirement. His wife suggested he has one year left, maybe two, leaving the league in familiar suspense about when the 40-year-old Russian legend will finally hang up his skates. Across the league, the 2026 free agency frenzy rolls on, with general managers burning phone lines and cap space in equal measure as rosters transform daily.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILDLY AS TEAMS REMAKE ROSTERS FOR 2026
story.deck: Three franchises swap signal-callers in a chaotic May that is reshaping the NFC landscape.
story.body:
The NFL offseason turned frantic this week as the Carolina Panthers, Cleveland Browns, and New Orleans Saints all confirmed quarterback moves that will define their franchises for years to come. Carolina agreed to terms with former Las Vegas Raiders starter Gardner Minshew on a two-year, $38 million deal, betting the journeyman veteran can stabilize an offense that cycled through three starters during the 2025 season. Panthers general manager Dan Morgan called Minshew a proven leader whose toughness fits the culture the organization is trying to rebuild from the ground up.

In Cleveland, the Browns pulled off the most surprising move of the spring, sending a second-round pick to the Pittsburgh Steelers in exchange for backup quarterback Kyle Allen, then turning around and naming him the Week 1 starter over holdover Dorian Thompson-Robinson. The deal stunned observers around the league who expected Cleveland to address the position in next month's supplemental draft or via free agency rather than trading for an unproven option. Browns head coach Kevin Stefanski defended the move at the team's voluntary minicamp Tuesday, arguing that Allen's familiarity with coordinator Ken Dorsey's system gives Cleveland the best chance to compete in a wide-open AFC North.

The Saints, meanwhile, completed a blockbuster trade with the Tennessee Titans to acquire veteran Derek Carr's former backup, moving two mid-round picks to land a starter they believe can win immediately in a retooled offense under new coordinator Klint Kubiak. New Orleans also used the fourth overall pick in April's draft to select Ohio State offensive tackle Josh Simmons, giving the franchise its most promising offensive line prospect since Andrus Peat. League analysts noted that the Saints roster, bolstered by the February retirement of aging receiver Chris Olave's replacement and a healthy return of running back Alvin Kamara, looks more balanced heading into training camp than at any point in the last three seasons.
